newsitem.title: ROMANIA: World Bank agrees $625 million in Romania credits.
newsitem.headline: World Bank agrees $625 million in Romania credits.

text.p: The World Bank boosted its 1997 package of credits to Romania to $625 million on Monday and the Bank's president called the increase a reward for the new reformist government's progress in introducing reforms.
"Maybe this is a prize for good performance," James Wolfensohn told a news conference after a day of talks with the Balkan country's centrist leaders.
"The government suggested it wanted more money and more money up front. We thought that was reasonable and did it."

The centrist coalition, which ended seven years of leftist rule in last November's election, launched its reform programme in February and last month won $430 million in credits from the International Monetary Fund.

The World Bank credits included $350 million for reforming the loss-making farm sector, $50 million to underpin social benefits and cushion the effects of rapid change, $150 million to upgrade potholed roads, $50 million for higher education and $25 million to improve water supplies.
A further $80 million was likely to be approved within a week under a resumed disbursement of an earlier loan aimed at restructuring enterprises.
Earlier World Bank proposals had provided for about $300 million plus the resumed enterprise funds.
Wolfensohn said disbursement of more than $300 million would occur this year. All the credits must be approved by the Bank's board next month.

He said measures undertaken by the government "were almost out of a textbook in terms of restructuring the economy, changing the legal system, the goals of the financial sector, monetary policy and the judicial system".
The credits package, he said, was "a real sign of our confidence in the country, particularly the front-loading of funds to this extent".
Both the World Bank and IMF suspended credits last year after complaining that the leftist government of the time had overspent in an election year and was too slow in implementing market measures.
The new government has been pressing on in recent weeks with measures to tackle issues viewed by international lenders as roadblocks to credits.
At the weekend, the cabinet approved new legislation altering banking regulations and drew up a list of 75 state-run farms to be privatised or shut down.
